lesson.title: Mirror Images: Reflecting Functions
lesson.summary: A reflection flips a graph over the x-axis or y-axis, producing a mirror image with a negated input or output.
lesson.body:
A reflection is a transformation that flips a graph over a line, most commonly the x-axis or the y-axis, producing a mirror image of the original shape on the opposite side of that line. Unlike a translation, which slides a graph to a new location without altering it, a reflection changes the graph's orientation: a shape that opened upward can end up opening downward, or a shape that increased from left to right can end up decreasing instead. Reflections are produced by attaching a negative sign to a function, either in front of it or inside it.

Reflecting over the x-axis flips a graph vertically and is written g(x) = -f(x), which negates every output: any point (x, y) on the original graph becomes (x, -y) on the reflected graph. Reflecting over the y-axis flips a graph horizontally instead and is written g(x) = f(-x), which negates the input before evaluating the parent function: any point (x, y) becomes (-x, y). These are genuinely different transformations, and mixing them up is one of the most common errors when graphing.

Consider the function f(x) = x^2 - 4x, which factors as f(x) = x(x - 4), so it crosses the x-axis at x = 0 and x = 4. Reflect it over the x-axis to get g(x) = -f(x) = -(x^2 - 4x) = -x^2 + 4x. First evaluate the original at x = 1: f(1) = 1 - 4 = -3. The reflected function should give the opposite output at the same input: g(1) = -x^2 + 4x evaluated at x = 1 gives -(1) + 4(1) = -1 + 4 = 3, and indeed 3 is the opposite of -3, confirming the vertical flip worked correctly.

Now reflect the original f(x) = x^2 - 4x over the y-axis instead, giving h(x) = f(-x) = (-x)^2 - 4(-x) = x^2 + 4x. This time the rule says h(1) should equal f(-1), since reflecting over the y-axis means the output at x = 1 matches whatever the original function produced at x = -1. Check both sides: h(1) = 1^2 + 4(1) = 1 + 4 = 5, and directly, f(-1) = (-1)^2 - 4(-1) = 1 + 4 = 5. The two calculations agree, confirming the horizontal flip.

Reflections can also combine: applying both a negative sign in front of a function and a negative sign inside it, g(x) = -f(-x), flips the graph over both axes at once, which is the same as rotating the original graph 180 degrees around the origin. For the absolute value parent f(x) = |x|, this double reflection gives g(x) = -|-x| = -|x|, an upside-down V that opens downward instead of the usual upward V, since |-x| always equals |x| for any real number x.

Reflections, translations, and the stretches and compressions from the general transformation equation together make up the complete toolkit for reshaping a parent function into any member of its family, and recognizing which combination of these has been applied to a graph is often the fastest way to sketch a complicated-looking function without plotting dozens of individual points.
